output.diagnosis: Use customer research and implementation of well-supported fixes now; do not run a conventional A/B test. At 20 purchases/month, the store is below the under-30-orders/month gate where statistically credible A/B tests are not practical. With 1,500 sessions/month, even large purchase-conversion effects would take too long to evaluate reliably, and small UI tests would be especially uninformative.
actions: Instrument the funnel before changing pages: capture device, channel/source, landing page, product page views, add-to-cart, begin checkout, purchase, errors, payment failures, shipping-cost exposure, and coupon use. Verify analytics and ecommerce events reconcile with actual orders.
Review the highest-traffic paths first: homepage or primary landing page, top product-detail pages, cart, and checkout. Do not spend effort optimizing low-traffic category pages.

Run qualitative research to identify friction and objections: 5-8 moderated usability sessions with people matching the target customer; watch them find a product, assess suitability, understand routine/ingredients, and attempt checkout.

Interview recent purchasers and non-purchasers. Ask what problem they wanted to solve, what alternatives they considered, what nearly stopped them, what made them trust the product, and what information was missing. Avoid leading questions about proposed design changes.
Add a short on-site exit or post-purchase survey. For non-buyers, ask their main reason for not buying; for buyers, ask what nearly prevented purchase and why they chose this brand.

Review session recordings and funnel drop-offs once tracking is in place. Look for repeated behaviors such as ingredient/safety uncertainty, unclear skin-type fit, weak product-routine guidance, shipping/returns surprise, discount-code hunting, navigation loops, or checkout errors.

Make high-confidence repairs and best-practice improvements without A/B testing—for example, clarify product benefits and use cases, skin-type suitability, ingredients and directions, proof/reviews, shipping and returns, routine/bundle guidance, and checkout friction—but prioritize only issues supported by research or obvious defects.

Maintain an experiment/learning log: observed evidence, hypothesis, change made, date, traffic mix, and downstream metrics. Monitor add-to-cart and begin-checkout as directional leading indicators, while retaining purchases and revenue as guardrails.

When monthly orders consistently exceed 30, consider one bold, pre-planned A/B test at a time on the highest-traffic page. Use a frequent micro-conversion as the primary metric and purchase/revenue as guardrails; avoid button-color, copy-only, or other small-MDE tests.
missing_information: Device breakdown and device-specific funnel conversion rates.
Traffic-source mix, including paid email/SMS, organic, affiliates, and returning versus new visitors.
Which pages receive the 1,500 monthly sessions and traffic to each top product page, cart, and checkout.
Current conversion rates for product view to add-to-cart, add-to-cart to checkout, and checkout to purchase.
Top products, price points, shipping cost/thresholds, delivery times, returns policy, and current offers.
Whether checkout has technical, payment, address, inventory, discount-code, or mobile usability errors.
Availability of analytics, session replay, survey tools, consent coverage, and ability to recruit customers/prospects for research.
Whether conversion varies materially by product, geography, campaign, or seasonality.
caveats: The recommendation is based on the supplied 20 monthly purchases and 1,500 monthly sessions; device or channel concentration could change where research should focus, but does not make a standard purchase-based A/B program well powered at this order volume.
Do not treat a short before/after change as proof of causation. Promotions, weekday mix, seasonality, creative changes, email/SMS sends, and traffic-source shifts can explain changes.
Micro-conversions are useful for diagnosing behavior, but an increase in add-to-cart or checkout starts does not necessarily produce more purchases or revenue.
If a future test produces an unexpectedly large apparent winner, validate it with a holdout or replication before assuming the revenue gain is durable.
Avoid unplanned daily significance checks or stopping a future test when results first look favorable; this increases false-positive risk.

input.task: Should we run an A/B test or use customer research to improve conversion?
input.brand: DTC skincare store; 1500 sessions and 20 purchases per month; no device breakdown yet.
input.knowledge:
[a1e60a3f49fe31eb99644d68] Low-traffic playbook: test bigger, not more
Use when: Running an experimentation programme for a store that cannot power small-MDE tests.
- Change the goal: below the A/B power threshold, the job shifts from proving things statistically to learning fast and cheaply. Test bigger, not more.
- Default to differentiated changes with a target effect of 10-20%+ below about 100,000 visitors/month, not tweaks. VWO concedes low-traffic sites should make big changes; one bold homepage test teaches more than 10 micro-tests on low-traffic category pages (SplitBase).
- Concentrate tests where the traffic is: homepage, top product pages, cart. Do not test low-traffic category pages.
- Use micro-conversions (add-to-cart, begin-checkout) as the primary metric because they are more frequent and power faster — but a lift in add-to-cart may not carry through to purchase or revenue, so keep purchase and revenue as guardrails and use the micro-conversion as a leading indicator.
- Use sequential before/after with honest error bars only when parallel testing is impossible and you can hold external conditions constant; it is best for large structural changes and should be treated as weak evidence.
- Lead with qualitative research (session replay, surveys, user testing, customer interviews) to generate strong hypotheses when you cannot run many tests.
- Re-test any surprising large winner with a holdout before banking the revenue.
Caveat: Before/after confounds the change with time — seasonality, promotions, weekday/weekend, traffic-source shifts, news. The real problem is bias, not just wider variance.
Caveat: The source does not define a metric for 'teaches more' when preferring one bold test.

[4d9d95179f67b0001d0ff96c] Stage-gated experimentation playbook by monthly order volume
Use when: Deciding what kind of testing programme your store can honestly run at its current volume.
- Assume a DTC context: roughly 2-3% site conversion rate and mostly new/anonymous traffic. Orders per month is the binding constraint because conversions per variant drive power.
- Under 30 orders/month: valid are qualitative research only (session replay, surveys, user testing, customer interviews, analytics funnel review), best-practice implementation of known fixes, and repairs. Not valid: any A/B test, A/B/n, bandits, or before/after with statistical claims — you cannot power even a 30% lift in a reasonable window (about 120+ conversions per variant needed). Do instead: fix what is broken, apply proven best practices without testing, build the research habit and an experiment log, interview customers.
- 30-300 orders/month: valid are bold big-swing A/B tests on the highest-traffic page (home, hero product, cart), designed to detect 20%+ relative lifts over 2-4 weeks with a fixed pre-computed sample. Micro-conversion primary metrics with purchase as guardrail are valid; sequential before/after only for large structural changes with conditions held constant. Not valid: tweak tests needing a small MDE, A/B/n, revenue-per-visitor as primary (needs about 6x traffic), same-SKU price tests. Do instead: one big test at a time, research-heavy, sample-size calculator before every test.
- 300-3,000 orders/month: valid are regular A/B tests targeting 10-20% lifts on high-traffic pages with conversion rate as primary and guardrails on AOV/margin/return rate, two-week minimum runtime and SRM checks; use sequential or always-valid engines (Statsig, GrowthBook, Eppo, Optimizely) so you can monitor without peeking penalties. Borderline: RPV as primary, A/B/n with 2-3 arms, CUPED if you have returning identified users. Not valid: detecting sub-5% lifts, many simultaneous variants, same-SKU price tests.
- 3,000-20,000 orders/month: valid are A/B/n, bandits for short campaigns and tactical high-volume decisions, RPV with winsorization, CUPED, pre-registered segment analysis, and device/source splits. Detecting 5-10% lifts becomes feasible on hero pages. Not valid: reliably detecting sub-2-3% lifts without long runtimes; same-SKU price discrimination. Do instead: run a proper programme with server-side checkout/pricing testing (Plus), hybrid A/B plus bandit, formal guardrails and stopping rules.
- 20,000+ orders/month: valid are small-MDE tests (2-5%), revenue and gross-profit-per-visitor primaries, CUPED and variance reduction, always-valid sequential monitoring, multiple concurrent experiments with FDR control, bandits for personalisation, holdouts for surprising winners, and long-term novelty/primacy analysis. Not valid: naive same-SKU price discrimination, unplanned peeking, uncorrected multiple comparisons. Do instead: operate like Booking or Microsoft in miniature — institutional experiment log, replication of surprising results, A/A tests to validate the platform, and a culture that expects most tests to fail.
Caveat: The bands assume the stated 2-3% conversion rate and mostly anonymous traffic; a store with very different dynamics should recompute.
Caveat: Bandit use below the 3,000 orders/month gate is defensible only for short regret-minimising campaigns.

[a8e9574ba919a3f87d6a69bb] Choose big swings or comprehensive CRO based on monthly sessions
Use when: Deciding whether to invest in micro A/B tests or larger redesigns/offer tests for an ecommerce store.
- Use the source's internal benchmark: under 300,000 sessions per month, focus on much bigger swings rather than micro A/B tests (button color, above-fold image swaps, small text changes).
- For brands under 300,000 sessions, the source lists big-swing levers including landing page design concepts, PDP redesigns based on data, offer and price testing month to month, free-shipping and price tests in cart/checkout, post-purchase upsells and surveys, and creative-to-landing-page alignment.
- Over 300,000 sessions — assuming conversion rate and order volume are good enough to produce enough data — run comprehensive CRO: deep qualitative and quantitative audits, isolated A/B tests, higher experiment velocity (the source cites four to eight A/B tests per month), a full data stack (GA4, heatmaps, surveys, session recordings), a roadmap, learning loops from wins and losses, and cross-functional teamwork.
- Note the source explicitly revised this threshold in light of harder attribution and rising CPMs, so treat 300,000 as a situational internal benchmark, not a universal law.
- The source says under the threshold you need an agency or must invest the time and resource yourself to run the essential analyses.
Caveat: 300,000 monthly sessions is described as an internal benchmark that changed in the last six to 12 months, not a proven universal cutoff.
Caveat: 'Good enough' conversion rate and 'enough orders' are not defined.
Caveat: The source says there are six to eight big-swing items but does not enumerate a clean list; the count is inconsistent.

[9ba46f7b06eef08a032ed60c] Decide whether a real A/B test is even feasible
Use when: Before signing off a CRO test plan, hiring an agency, or claiming a test win.
- Work out the sessions needed. To trust a 10-20% conversion lift, the source estimates roughly 1,000 conversions per variant; at a 2.5% conversion rate that is about 40,000 sessions per variant, or 80,000 sessions for a simple 50/50 split.
- Check whether your brand can actually generate that volume on a single product page in a month; the source says most seven-figure brands cannot.
- Do not peek daily and stop when it looks significant: this substantially inflates the false positive rate, so even tests that look valid often are not.
- Control contamination. Klaviyo campaigns cause artificial spikes in conversion and revenue; if that traffic can reach the test pages it can wreck the test.
- Run tests on custom landing pages fed only cold Meta traffic rather than forking traffic on the live site.
- Account for multi-click journeys: the source says Meta users average about 1.5 clicks before converting, so roughly half of buyers take more than one click and may be exposed to both test cells.
Caveat: The conversion and session figures are the source's estimates for illustration, not a universal requirement.
Caveat: The source still endorses A/B testing and CRO agencies; it argues the program needs enough session volume and a category where time-to-purchase is short.
Caveat: The 1.5-click figure is from the source's work with large brands, not a general benchmark.
